The two primary goals of this modeling effort are to determine the stress margin in the tank, and to determine dynamics of the seal as it deforms under compression. This simulates the sealing process, which is critical to maintaining vacuum and the thermal integrity of the tank. Page 9 of 30 Approved for Public Release Figure 8 (a) Finite element model of the inner tank, and (b) close-up of the boss parts and their connection to the tank Continuum-shell elements of type ‘SC8R’ were used to model the tank. This element type provides the flexibility of allowing the user to easily change/apply different ply directions to determine an optimal ply orientation (as with shells elements), and at the same time, be able to capture through-thickness stresses at the location of flanges due to compressive loads- which shells either cannot capture effectively (thin shells) or with low accuracy (thick shells). The mesh of the tank and boss parts are shown in Figure 9. The cool-down portion of the analysis (the second load-case) was simulated isothermally, i.e. a temperature profile was applied to the tank in 4 zones of varying temperatures. A transient heat transfer analysis was not performed as a part of this analysis. The model, as it stands, has several complexities including multi-body contact between the flanges, the anchor, tank, seal and cushion, in addition to a ply-by-ply description of the tank. To keep the model complexity tractable, a coupled thermal-structural approach was not taken here. Cooling was assumed to be iso-thermal, as a preliminary step, with temperature profiles taken from a separate transient analysis, and simplified into 4 zones, where temperature in each zone is uniform. The model and results are described further below. Details of the model, BCs and material properties are also mentioned in the conference presentation [3]. Figure 9 Mesh details of the composite inner tank, upper bulkhead, seal and cushion The tank had minimal boundary conditions that allow it full freedom to contract/deform as needed. Boundary conditions for the tank are shown in Figure 10. During preliminary runs of the model, some instability/lack of convergence was observed, and this was believed to be due to (small) motion of the tank itself (a long Page 10 of 30 Approved for Public Release structure). This being a quasi-static, implicit analysis, no stabilization from mass/inertia of the model was present. To address this, springs with a very low stiffness were applied to the bottom of the tank, as shown in Figure 10 (a). Stresses in this portion of tank were examined after analysis and seen to be very low, and hence it is concluded that these springs do not affect the primary nature of the result, which was stresses in the tank near the boss, which is at the other end of the tank, and in the central portion of the tank.
